Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act aims to unleash renewable energy, lower emissions and electricity costs, and fight climate change

Pawtucket, RI – Today, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (EPW), and Jay Timmons, President of the National Association of Manufacturers (NAM), convened a roundtable with leaders from Rhode Island’s manufacturing, labor, and business communities to discuss Whitehouse’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The roundtable followed a tour of the Cooley Group’s manufacturing facility in Pawtucket.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will deliver cheaper energy, more well-paying jobs, and responsible growth by accelerating the permitting and construction of critical energy and infrastructure projects while maintaining key environmental and historic preservation safeguards. The bipartisan legislation would bolster Rhode Island’s growing blue economy and clean energy industry, create loads of well-paying local union jobs, and build a more flexible energy grid that Rhode Island businesses and communities can rely on. BAAJA has received support from a broad national coalition of labor leaders, energy producers, and nonprofits.

“Rhode Islanders want lower energy bills and more well-paying union jobs. Passing this bipartisan bill will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy, make sure data centers start paying their fair share, and provide regulatory certainty to small businesses. A cleaner, safer, more abundant, and less expensive energy future awaits us on the other side of this permitting bill,” said Whitehouse, Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee. “The Trump administration must now end their mischief and show some real regulatory good faith to unlock the votes necessary to seal this deal.”

“Senator Whitehouse’s leadership in crafting and advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a breakthrough for manufacturing in America. He understands that manufacturers need certainty to build, grow and invest — and that once a permit is issued, a project should be able to move forward without years of unnecessary delays. Our broken permitting system costs manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually — resources we’d much rather spend on ribbon cuttings than red tape. Thanks to Senator Whitehouse’s leadership, we have a real opportunity to modernize this outdated system, unleash investment and create good-paying jobs while maintaining strong environmental protections and meaningful community engagement. Manufacturers are grateful for his unwavering commitment, and we’re proud to stand with him to get this bipartisan legislation across the finish line,” said Jay Timmons, President & CEO, National Association of Manufacturers.

The legislation was negotiated by Whitehouse along with U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Chairman of the EPW Committee; Mike Lee (R-UT), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee. It was unveiled late last month.

“The Cooley Team was pleased to welcome Senator Whitehouse to our Pawtucket operation and thanks NAM for bringing together this important discussion on permitting reform and the future of American manufacturing. Growth, job creation, and environmental stewardship can and should advance together. With leaders like the Senator championing bipartisan reform, we can encourage investment and hiring, expand access to affordable, reliable, cleaner energy, and maintain strong environmental protections,” said Dan Dwight, President & CEO, Cooley Group and NAM Executive Committee Member.

“We need Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act right away. There is no time to lose when it comes to passing a bill of this magnitude to create good union jobs and lower families’ energy bills,” said Michael F. Sabitoni, General Secretary-Treasurer of the Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA). “This legislation is an example of what leaders in Washington can accomplish when they set differences aside to work across the aisle and improve the lives of working men and women across the country.”

“The only way we are truly create a cleaner and greener economic future is to build new renewable energy infrastructure. We can no longer be held back by a permitting regime designed to thwart that development. The Rhode Island labor movement is leading on climate, and this proposal goes a long way towards helping Rhode Island meet its Act on Climate goals,” said Patrick Crowley, President, RI AFL-CIO.

“For U.S. manufacturers, access to reliable, affordable energy is essential to remaining competitive, creating jobs, and driving economic growth. This bipartisan permitting reform legislation represents one of the most significant efforts in decades to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, modernize our electric grid, expand energy supply, and accelerate critical infrastructure investments. We commend Senator Sheldon Whitehouse for his leadership in advancing reforms that will strengthen grid reliability, help reduce energy costs, and ensure American manufacturers have the energy infrastructure necessary to innovate, grow, and compete globally,” said Melissa Travis, President & CEO, Rhode Island Manufacturers Association (RIMA).

“For Rhode Island businesses, time is money – and lengthy and unpredictable permitting processes can stall a project or send it to another state entirely,” said Liz Catucci, executive director for The Partnership for Rhode Island. “The Partnership supports the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 because faster, more reliable permitting will help Rhode Island compete for the infrastructure and energy investments that create good-paying jobs here. We’re grateful for Senator Whitehouse’s leadership and willingness to work across the aisle on an issue that directly affects our businesses.”

“An outdated permitting process is holding up economic development in Rhode Island. Modernizing that system will help streamline energy, manufacturing, and infrastructure projects, bolster local small businesses, and create new jobs,” said Laurie White, President of the Greater Providence Chamber of Commerce. “I applaud the leadership of Senator Whitehouse and his bipartisan negotiating partners, and Congress should immediately prioritize passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.”

The bipartisan legislation provides greater certainty for projects that have already been permitted and financed, including by preventing future administrations from arbitrarily blocking entire classes of energy projects, while establishing clear timelines for environmental reviews and legal challenges. It also includes targeted reforms to expand and modernize the electric grid, speed the development of geothermal and other energy projects, and ensure that rapidly growing data centers pay the full cost of their associated transmission needs rather than passing those costs on to families and small businesses.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would:

Build more transmission, faster by strengthening the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC) “backstop” siting authority — giving the federal government stronger authority to approve power lines when a state rejects or does not act upon an application – and allowing applications for large lines to be processed simultaneously with state reviews, helping needed projects move through permitting faster.

Get more energy onto the grid by:

Requiring regional and interregional transmission planning that accounts for where new transmission is needed.

Requiring advanced transmission technologies, such as advanced conductors and grid-enhancing technologies, which make better use of the grid we already have.

Requiring coordinated generation interconnection and transmission planning – which is not happening in most areas of the country – and using computing technologies to evaluate requests to connect new energy projects to the grid, reducing the cost and speeding up the process of bringing new generation onto our grid.

Mandating that transmission planning organizations (RTOs and ISOs) allow aggregations of distributed energy resources to operate as virtual power plants and participate in wholesale electricity markets, helping meet growing demand with more available supply.

Requiring BLM to complete geothermal drilling permits and authorizations in 60 days and exempting low disturbance exploration and development activities from additional environmental reviews.

Force data centers pay their fair share by requiring data centers, and not American families and small businesses, to pay for their cost of service and upgrades to the transmission network; right now, data centers are only required to pay for service or upgrades, not both.

Create jobs across the energy supply chain by boosting the build out ofmore transmission, clean energy, supply manufacturing, and other grid infrastructure.

Create greater certainty for projects permitted and financed across administrations by prohibiting any administration from delaying or blocking permitting of a class of energy projects – meaning no administration can block all solar, wind, or other class of energy project permits without facing legal action and fines.

Set clear deadlines for environmental reviews — including a two-year deadline for Environmental Impact Statement reviews and a one-year deadline for Environmental Assessment reviews, with consequences for agencies that miss those deadlines. That means environmental reviews still happen, but not indefinitely.

Establish a new National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) consultation process that runs alongside National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews with a defined time limit, securing a statutory role for Tribes in determining how projects affect historic and cultural resources and protecting Tribes’ rights to formally consult during the processes — two things the Section 106 reforms attempted to eliminate.

Limit the types of impacts that projects are required to mitigate, creating clearer boundaries around which effects a project must mitigate or minimize.

Set clear limitations on when and how a project may be legally challenged.

Sets a 150-day deadline for legal challenges under the Clean Water Act (CWA), Endangered Species Act (ESA), NEPA, and NHPA.

Generally limits who can bring a legal challenge to people or groups that participated in the relevant comment period or Tribal consultation process.

Limits when a court can temporarily stop a project from moving forward, while preserving the existing ability to seek that relief under the Administrative Procedures Act.

Allow states to handle endangered species consultations when they have the capacity to do so. States with the demonstrated staffing, expertise, and resource capacity to take over certain wildlife-related consultations are permitted to do so.

Clarify the limits on state water-quality reviews by limiting state certifications to water pollution directly caused by a specific source for gas pipelines and transmission lines and prohibiting use of the process to address unrelated issues.

Prevent the federal government from changing the rules after the fact for certain wetlands and waterways by stopping EPA from preemptively or retroactively removing areas of land from the federal water-quality certification process.

Fund a first-of-its-kind Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund, providing a mandatory funding source dedicated to cleaning up abandoned hardrock mines.

Text of Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. — Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL), a member of the House Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust and U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) demanded answers from McDonald’s President and CEO Chris Kempczinski about how the company generates AI-driven pricing recommendations, whether McDonald’s pressures franchisees to follow them, and how the company assesses the technology’s potential harm to consumers and competition. The letter came after reports that the company is using artificial intelligence (AI) to determine the “optimal price” for individual menu items at each of its locations and pushing franchisees to adopt these AI-based prices.

“We are concerned that McDonald’s may be using AI to squeeze consumers into paying higher prices, and that its AI pricing tools may facilitate collusion between franchisees who should be operating as competitors,” wrote the lawmakers.

U.S. Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.), and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.) also signed the letter.

According to recent reports, McDonald’s has developed an AI-based pricing tool that it may be using to recommend specific prices for each individual store, building off the massive trove of consumer data that Amazon has collected through its loyalty program and mobile app. For example, two McDonald’s-operated restaurants just two miles apart in Fresno, California reportedly charged prices that differed by as much as 21 percent for the same menu items. The lawmakers raised particular concerns about McDonald’s use of AI-based pricing at a time when food prices are rising nationwide and particularly at McDonald’s. One report found that certain McDonald’s menu prices doubled between 2014 and 2024, rising more than three times as fast as overall inflation and driving away customers who previously relied on McDonald’s for an affordable meal.

“We are concerned that McDonald’s is using its extensive consumer data and algorithmic pricing tools to unfairly raise prices on consumers who are already struggling with high food and dining costs,” wrote the lawmakers.

The lawmakers also questioned McDonald’s for reportedly putting pressure on franchisees to adopt its pricing recommendations, including through new business standards and potential consequences for franchise renewals. They warned that encouraging competing franchisees to rely on a shared pricing tool informed by nonpublic data could undermine independent pricing decisions and raise antitrust concerns.

“While McDonald’s asserts that using data and analytics to inform pricing is a standard business practice, pressuring competing franchisees to use a shared AI pricing tool built on nonpublic data is not a standard business practice, but rather a potential antitrust issue,” continued the lawmakers.

The lawmakers requested answers by November 16, 2026, on the data and algorithms used to generate pricing recommendations, the extent to which franchisees adopt those recommendations, the pressure McDonald’s places on franchisees to comply, and the company’s assessment of potential antitrust risks.

Getting America Building Again

INTRODUCING A BLOG POST SERIES ON THE BIPARTISAN AMERICAN AFFORDABILITY AND JOBS ACT

America’s ambitions to strengthen energy security, reshore manufacturing, and lead the world in artificial intelligence depend on one fundamental capability: our ability to build. Yet regulatory uncertainty, prolonged reviews, and endless litigation have stalled critical infrastructure, driven up costs, and discouraged investment.

Drawing on four decades of private-sector experience, Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) has made permitting reform his top priority since joining the Senate in March. He introduced the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure (AEMI) Act, championed reform in his maiden Senate floor speech, and convened more than 150 stakeholders at a June Capitol Hill forum focused on America’s ability to build and compete.

Now, Congress is poised to meet the moment. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) have put forward the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026. Senator Armstrong has praised this bipartisan agreement for including meaningful reforms that would remove longstanding barriers to building critical infrastructure in this country. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has scheduled a procedural vote for November 9, when Congress returns to Washington—an opportunity to turn months of negotiations into legislative action.

That’s the focus of Getting America Building Again, a new blog series examining how the BAAJA will bring benefits including reducing costs, bringing regulatory certainty, and getting critical infrastructure built. Each installment will answer three questions:

The problem: What’s currently holding America back?

The solution: How would the bill address it?

The support: What are stakeholders across the country saying?

In this inaugural post, we note how the need for permitting reform—and the bipartisan agreement to deliver it—has united an extraordinary coalition spanning industry, utilities, advocacy organizations, and the policy community.

Leading business organizations have rallied behind the legislation. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce mobilized more than 850 organizations for comprehensive permitting reform and endorsed the Senate agreement, calling it “a once-in-a-generation opportunity to fix our broken permitting system.” More than 100 manufacturing and business organizations joined the National Association of Manufacturers in urging Congress to “swiftly pass” the bill, while Business Roundtable, the American Council for Capital Formation, and the Small Business & Entrepreneurship Council issued independent endorsements.

Energy providers and industry associations have also lined up behind the bill. The nation’s consumer-owned utilities, represented by the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) and American Public Power Association (APPA), expressed “strong support” in a joint letter. Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA) endorsed it. Leading clean-energy associations—including the Solar Energy Industry Alliance (SEIA), American Clean Power Association (ACP), Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA), and Advanced Energy United—also jointly urged passage, underscoring the importance of permitting reform to expanding electricity supply and modernizing the grid.

Conservative organizations have mobilized, too. Pacific Legal Foundation led more than 35 groups in sending a letter of support, while Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions and SAFE led a separate 15-group coalition letter. Groups that individually endorsed or publicly expressed support for the legislation include: ACC Action, ClearPath Action, Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions, Club for Growth, Conservative Energy Network, Americans for Prosperity, and Pacific Legal Foundation. Cato Institute’s Travis Fisher and Michael Abi-Nader called it an “excellent set of bipartisan reforms.” Foundation for American Innovation’s Thomas Hochman said that BAAJA would be “if passed, the most consequential energy legislation in decades.”

Support also extends across center-left policy organizations and climate advocates. Bipartisan Policy Center Action, the Breakthrough Institute, and Citizens’ Climate Lobby have endorsed the legislation. Inclusive Abundance Action called it “a huge bipartisan win,” while Chamber of Progress described it as “better than most of us could have predicted.” Third Way welcomed “meaningful progress” toward affordable, reliable electricity, and the Progressive Policy Institute applauded a “major bipartisan breakthrough.” The ACORE called the bill “an essential step” toward accelerating clean energy and transmission, while Ceres also praised its provisions to accelerate infrastructure development and modernize the grid.

Even as some environmental groups oppose the compromise, prominent clean-energy and center-left voices are making the case for passage. Climate investor Tom Steyer appealed directly to fellow progressives: “this is a bill we should support, and I’m asking you to join me.” Third Way’s Josh Freed criticized groups “more interested in obstructing imperfect solutions than working to improve them.” Searchlight Institute’s Jane Flegal and Pavan Venkatakrishnan argued that the bill would help unlock clean-energy construction at scale, while Columbia University’s Jason Bordoff warned that rejecting the deal over its potential benefits for fossil fuels would squander an opportunity to advance energy security, affordability, and clean energy.

The stakes are clear, the support is broad, and Congress has an opportunity to act. In the installments ahead, we’ll examine what’s holding America back, how the bipartisan agreement addresses those obstacles, and why a growing choir of stakeholders are calling for reform.

It’s time to get America building again.

America Has the Energy. Permitting Reform Can Help Make It Affordable.

HOW THE BAAJA WILL LOWER ENERGY COSTS AND PROTECT RATEPAYERS

America has the energy resources to meet growing demand. But permitting bottlenecks delay the pipelines, power plants, and transmission lines needed to deliver them—constraining supply and raising costs. The bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act addresses both challenges: make it easier to build affordable energy infrastructure and protect existing customers from costs driven by major new electricity users.

THE PROBLEM WITH THE STATUS QUO

New England illustrates the consequences of not building. Although the United States is the world’s largest natural gas producer, pipeline constraints limit access to nearby Pennsylvania gas. During a January 2026 cold snap, oil overtook natural gas as the region’s leading source of electricity. When affordable fuel cannot reach consumers, more expensive alternatives fill the gap.

The costs extend nationwide. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce estimates that permitting delays are holding up as much as $1.5 trillion in critical infrastructure investment. Meanwhile, research commissioned by the Corporate Energy Buyers Association finds that restricting new wind and solar development could add $121.2 billion to U.S. energy expenses from 2027 through 2033. Whether the obstacle is a pipeline or a power line, limiting supply means fewer options and higher costs.

HOW THE BIPARTISAN BILL HELPS

The bill addresses both the cost of building infrastructure and who pays for it. As the Bipartisan Policy Center explains, it would streamline pipelines and transmission development, accelerate connections for new generation and storage, and expand capacity on the existing grid. Faster construction and more available supply can reduce costs. The bill would also require covered data centers to pay infrastructure costs attributable to their expansion rather than shifting those costs onto existing customers.

Research points to substantial savings:

The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates that achieving the bill’s envisioned two-year environmental-review deadline could reduce annual household electricity bills by 178–251.

The Rhodium Group projects 50–78 in annual household electricity bill savings by 2040 from the bipartisan bill’s transmission, pipeline, and data-center provisions.

Resources for the Future estimates more than $350 billion in cumulative electricity-system savings through 2050 from modeled provisions of the bill.

C2ES and Greenline Insights project roughly $19 billion in residential savings through 2040 from comparable transmission and interconnection reforms.

While the studies examine different provisions and scenarios, they point in the same direction: building infrastructure faster and using the grid more efficiently can lower electricity costs.

WHO SUPPORTS IT — AND WHY

The affordability case spans industries and energy sources. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce argues that modernizing permitting can unlock investment and lower everyday costs. Enbridge CEO Greg Ebel put it simply: “If we can’t build it, we can’t afford it.” Corporate Energy Buyers Association CEO Rich Powell called for “the low-cost, reliable power” Americans need. Advanced Energy United CEO Heather O’Neill says reform can “tamp down energy costs,” while Solar Energy Industries Association CEO Tim Pawlenty anticipates “downward pressure on energy prices.”

Utilities agree. “Permitting reform is not a partisan issue. It is an affordability issue,” said American Gas Association CEO Karen Harbert. The American Public Power Association and National Rural Electric Cooperative Association have endorsed the bill, with APPA CEO Scott Corwin emphasizing the need to “keep electricity affordable” while maintaining reliability.

Support also crosses ideological lines. Club for Growth President David McIntosh sees a path to “lowering energy costs for families and businesses.” Inclusive Abundance Action President Derek Kaufman calls for “more power, built faster, at a price people can afford.” The Climate Leadership Council stresses building fast enough to meet demand, while Natural Allies’ Susan Waller sees a “generational opportunity to make energy more affordable.” The American Consumer Institute’s Kristen Walker warns that the status quo is “actively undermining affordability and reliability.”

Organized labor is making the same argument. LIUNA General President Brent Booker says the bill will “lower energy costs for all Americans.” Operating Engineers General President John Downey highlights putting skilled workers to work while “making energy more affordable and reliable for American families.” United Association General President Mark McManus likewise emphasizes delivering “reliable and affordable energy to American communities.”

“Early on, it was evident that this was going to be a very unique election,” said Senator Martin Heinrich, (D) New Mexico.

As the financial system accelerates, real-time information and automated tools can help institutions and regulators respond faster, improve access to liquidity, and better prepare for orderly bank resolutions. Meanwhile, advances in AI are creating new cybersecurity threats. Through enhanced collective maintenance and security built in from the start, open-source software can provide stronger protection against cyber threats. The Real-Time Regulatory Study Act directs the Federal Reserve Board, in coordination with other financial regulators, to develop, test, and publicly release open-source demonstration software to evaluate how technology can streamline regulatory obligations, reduce compliance costs, and provide regulators with real-time information on the condition of financial institutions nationwide. NOBLESVILLE, IN — Congresswoman Victoria Spartz (IN-05) is calling for sweeping federal and state investigations into utility surcharges, corporate subsidies, energy infrastructure costs, threats to grid reliability, and the use of eminent domain for projects benefiting private corporations.

In three letters to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and Department of Energy (DOE), and Indiana’s new legislative leadership, Spartz is demanding independent audits, stronger property rights, greater transparency, and meaningful regulatory reforms.

“Americans are being forced to bankroll a system where powerful utilities collect guaranteed returns, wealthy corporations receive massive subsidies, and hardworking families and small businesses get stuck with higher bills,” said Rep. New analyses of a permitting reform bill U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) has championed say that its provisions would reduce emissions and costs to ratepayers, as well as recover billions of dollars from data center developers.

The analyses, released separately in recent days by four independent nonprofit and industry groups, including the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, modeled what would happen to energy transmission and green energy production with and without Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in effect through 2040.

They found that the bill would lower household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040. Moreover, it would reduce power sector emissions by about 20%, which would subsequently help prevent approximately 6,700 deaths and save $54 billion in cumulative public health costs.

Heinrich, the ranking member of the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee, announced the proposal along with Chair U.S. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and other bipartisan senators in recent weeks. He has touted the bill as a way to reform the federal permit review process to reduce delays and give renewable energy developers more certainty and quicker reviews, as well as a way to ensure data center developers don’t pass energy costs onto nearby households.

The bill has received backlash from tribal and environmentalist groups concerned it will fast-track fossil fuel production and reduce tribal input on sensitive developments. Last week, protesters from the YUCCA Alliance railed against the bill outside Heinrich’s downtown Albuquerque office.

But Heinrich has maintained the bill will prevent vital carbon-free energy and transmission projects from facing years of regulatory delays. His office has pointed to the analyses as proof the bill is necessary to achieve climate goals.

“Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years,” Heinrich said in a statement touting the outside reviews. “These independent analyses show exactly what we stand to gain by fixing our broken permitting system: lower electricity bills, cleaner air, healthier communities, and more reliable energy infrastructure.”

One of those reviews, released Thursday by the nonpartisan Center for Climate and Energy Solutions thinktank, found that passing the bill would reduce annual electricity bills by $2.5 billion by 2035, partially by reducing the queue that power plants, energy storage facilities and energy storage projects idle in before getting approval to connect to the grid.

“It takes years for projects to connect to the grid and be able to deliver that energy,” the center’s president, Nat Keohane, said during a virtual news conference. “When demand is growing and supply can’t keep up, costs go up.”

A separate analysis from Grid Strategies, a power sector consulting firm, evaluated provisions in the 417-page bill related to data centers. The bill would require electrical utilities to impose additional costs on data centers, funding that utilities would then use to reduce transmission costs to ratepayers.

In total, Grid Strategies estimates that data centers would pay $55 billion to utilities over the next decade if the bill goes into effect, a figure that represents an additional $35 billion more than they would pay under existing policy.

Heinrich and his cosponsors have announced they intend to try to shepherd the bill through both chambers of Congress before the next session begins next year. U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) announced last week that she does not support the bill as written.

The bill sponsors’ push to pass the bill in 2026 has drawn additional criticism from the bill’s skeptics, who argue Democrats’ new majorities in the U.S. Senate and U.S. House in Tuesday’s election means a better bill can be achieved.

Moreover, in January, Heinrich may take over as chair of the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee, giving him even more power over the bill’s provisions.

However, in an emailed statement Thursday provided to Source NM, Heinrich said he still thinks the climate and country can’t wait any longer to pass the permitting reform bill. He said if he becomes committee chair that his priorities will be reducing energy costs for New Mexicans and protecting public lands, including in Chaco Canyon and the Pecos River.

“But our priority right now is passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would make it illegal for data centers to shift the costs of their grid upgrades and infrastructure onto consumers,” he said. “We’ve been working toward permitting reform for the better part of a decade, and this is the closest we’ve come to getting something signed into law. I’m not going to wait, and I’ll negotiate in good faith, whether I’m the Chair or the Ranking Member.”

WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released a fact sheet detailing how his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will hold data centers accountable, forcing them to pay for grid upgrades instead of passing costs onto electricity customers, helping to lower utility bills for working families.

Heinrich’s fact sheet can be found here and below.

Bipartisan American Affordability & Jobs Act

Making sure data centers pay for their grid costs, lowering utility bills for families

Large data centers can require as much electricity as a small city. When a data center connects to the grid, the utility may need to add or upgrade transmission infrastructure to serve that new demand. If those costs are not assigned to the data center, they can ultimately be reflected in electricity rates paid by other customers. A Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas working paper estimates that data center demand has already pushed up wholesale electricity prices 6.9% nationally, a number that it projects could increase to 12.3% by 2028.

What The Bill Does:

Requires data centers to pay the costs they create. The bill directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to require utilities to establish rates that force large data centers to pay for both the cost of serving them and the grid upgrades needed to handle them. This means the cost of accommodating a new data center does not fall on other electricity customers.

Ends a current barrier to charging data centers for grid upgrades. Current FERC policy generally prevents utilities from charging customers for both their share of existing grid costs and the additional grid upgrades needed to serve that customer. The bill directs FERC to change that policy to ensure that large data centers pay for both. If a data center needs the grid to be expanded or upgraded to power its operations, utilities must charge customers serving that data center for those costs on top of the regular cost of electricity. The bill makes these charges mandatory—not voluntary—ultimately driving down costs for consumers.

Gives states a way to reduce costs for families and businesses. States can use the revenue collected from data centers to reduce electricity rates for homes, small businesses, and other existing electricity customers.

Requires the reporting of information on data center energy usage. Requires the Energy Information Administration to update its annual survey to require utilities to report electricity sales to data centers—which utilities currently report for residential, commercial, and industrial sectors, but not for data centers.

With U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley

Q: What’s on Congress’ plate before the end of the year?

A: With the midterm elections behind us, the 119th Congress returns to Washington with a plate of unfinished business to address. That includes passing the annual defense authorization bill, keeping the government open beyond the short-term funding bill that expires on Dec. 11 and reauthorizing key rural healthcare programs, including the Medicare-dependent and low-volume hospital programs, Rural Community Hospital Demonstration Program and a Medicare payment floor for rural doctors and clinics. For 65 years in a row, Congress has worked across the aisle to pass the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The annual legislation sets defense-related policy and authorizes appropriations for the Pentagon, such as procurement for weapon systems, ships, and aircraft; payroll and personnel; military construction; and, nuclear weapons programs at the Department of Energy. The NDAA is often called must-pass legislation because it authorizes funding that supports military families, from housing to healthcare, and sets guidance on the nation’s defense programs that protect national security. It’s one of the most consequential bills every year on Congress’ to do list. For example, the fiscal year 2025 NDAA included 794 pages of policy measures and discretionary authorizations exceeding $883 billion. The bill is often a vehicle for other homeland security legislation to get passed. This year, I’ve filed bipartisan amendments to the NDAA that would protect kids online, fight organized crime and stem illicit drug use.

I’ll also be pushing to enact the five-year Farm Bill that’s been stalled for the last three years and operating under annual extensions. Unfortunately, Senate Democrats have refused to join Republican-led efforts to cut fraud from the food stamp program. Meanwhile, farmers need certainty and are counting on Congress to update conservation, rural development and farm credit policies that are operating under the 2018 farm law. I’m also committed to getting permanent, year-round nationwide E15 across the finish line that was included in the Farm Bill that passed the Senate Agriculture Committee. Getting E15 signed into law will help lower gas prices, boost corn demand and pump $14 billion into the farm economy. I’m hopeful lawmakers will reach a consensus once and for all to get the Farm Bill to the president’s desk before the end of the year.

Q: Why is permitting reform a bipartisan priority?

A: There is too much red tape in Washington. Public policies set decades ago to protect the environment are in dire need of an update to reflect changes in technology and address the regulatory and legal quagmire that’s standing in the way of bringing costs down for the American people. The federal permitting process that determines when and if critical infrastructure projects move from the drawing board to shovels in the ground is ineffective and costly. The heavy-handed bureaucratic review process is forcing American families to pay more for energy and consumer goods. Lawmakers on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee have rolled up their sleeves in good faith to hammer out a bipartisan bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It would reform the nation’s environmental review and federal permitting framework that’s driving up costs for Americans and impeding economic growth. By responsibly untangling the regulatory thicket that takes years and even decades for infrastructure projects to get started — from pipelines to transmission lines needed to boost the nation’s energy grid — Congress can fix the broken permitting process, better protect natural resources, pave the way for more affordable and reliable clean energy and foster economic development across the country. Importantly, the bill would help provide certainty to infrastructure projects that have received permitting approvals and secured financing by preventing future administrations from unwinding or blocking entire classes of energy projects. What’s more, the Senate bill would ensure data centers pay for their energy costs and protect families from footing the bill. For years, Congress has taken bites at the permitting reform apple. It’s time to get the job done and responsibly meet surging demand for affordable electricity so the U.S. economy isn’t left behind.

“I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration’s actions to develop data centers on public lands,” Heinrich began.

Heinrich’s letter follows his online post earlier today stating simply, “No data centers on public lands. Period.”

Heinrich's letter to Pearce comes after multiple actions from the Trump administration to develop data centers on public lands, including the June 2026 BLM approval of the 88-acre Townsite Data Center in Boulder City, Nevada. While the project was paused by the Department of the Interior’s Board of Land Appeals in September 2026, its approval was initially spurred by a 2025 Trump Executive Order that expedited the permitting of data center development on public lands.

BLM is now reportedly considering at least 15 proposals to build data centers or related infrastructure on public lands, covering more than 17,000 acres of public lands and stretching across six Western states. According to the Salt Lake Tribune, BLM asked state directors to identify public lands ready for data center development — something the Department of the Interior’s leadership told officials is a high priority.

“When BLM makes decisions about public land, it should always consider the best interest of the public and the communities that will be directly impacted by its decision,” Heinrich wrote.

“BLM should listen to the voices of the American people and carefully consider the many uses of public land before hastily greenlighting data center buildout on public lands,” Heinrich continued.

In the letter, Heinrich specifically requests a complete list of all authorities BLM is using to support data center development on public lands, all data center-related development proposals BLM is considering on public lands, and the public lands BLM has identified that are eligible for data center development.

Read the full letter here and below.

Director Pearce:

I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration’s actions to develop data centers on public lands.

In June 2026, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved the first data center on public lands—the sprawling 88-acre Townsite Data Center located in Boulder City, Nevada. At the time, BLM amended an existing right-of-way grant for a solar and battery-storage project to allow for the development of the data center. On September 1, following an appeal by Boulder City, Nevada, and environmental groups, the Department of the Interior’s Board of Land Appeals paused development of the data center, citing BLM’s decision to approve the project without conducting a new National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review. The Board found that Boulder City and the environmental groups “made a persuasive showing that BLM violated NEPA and acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is ‘substantially the same’ as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis.”

BLM’s decision to approve the Townsite Data Center followed an Executive Order signed by President Trump in July 2025 that expedited the permitting of data centers on public lands. In September, the President signed another Executive Order that grants Secretary Burgum additional independent authorities over energy production on public lands. BLM is now reportedly considering at least 15 proposals to build data centers or related infrastructure on public lands. The development proposals cover more than 17,000 acres of public lands and stretch across six western states. According to a report, BLM recently asked state directors to identify public lands ready for data center development and the Department of the Interior’s leadership told officials that the topic is high priority.

When BLM makes decisions about public land, it should always consider the best interest of the public and the communities that will be directly impacted by its decision. The Multiple Use – Sustained Yield principle of public land management requires the BLM to consider the other uses of public land when considering whether to site a data center in any specific location. BLM should listen to the voices of the American people and carefully consider the many uses of public land before hastily greenlighting data center buildout on public lands.

A complete list of all authorities BLM is using to support data center development on public lands. Please include the specific precedent and legal rationale.

A complete list of all data center related development proposals BLM is considering on public lands. For each proposal, please include the specific entity that is backing the project; the precise location of the project; the total acreage of federally owned land under review for development; the precise use of the federally owned land under review for development (e.g., for transmission lines, roads, or physical data center structures); whether the review will entail a NEPA review, or in the case of an existing right-of-way grant, a new NEPA review; and whether the proposal will have a public comment period.

A complete list of all public lands BLM has identified that are eligible for data center development.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this request. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact my staff at (202) 224-4971.

Sincerely,

“The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of AI,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers continued, “As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products. With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary. On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.”

The lawmakers continued, “Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders, it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. The lawmakers also raised concerns about the CPSC’s intention to expand data collection under the NEISS-R program, “Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction. Based on public reporting, the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.”

The lawmakers continued, “Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be ‘quite lethal’, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.”

The lawmakers called on CPSC to halt the implementation of NIESS-R in light of privacy concerns and a lack of transparency involving its implementation process “The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data…Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R.”

The full text of today’s letter is available here and below.

Dear Acting Chair Feldman,

We are deeply troubled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s (CPSC) decision to continue with the expansion of the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) without providing detailed information about its rollout to the public or to Congress. The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI).[1]

As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products.[2] With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary.[3] On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.[4] Under the Paperwork Reduction Act, the CPSC is obligated to submit a Federal Register notice and set up a public comment period along with publishing a System of Records notice before making this change.[5] Despite this legal requirement, the Commission has yet to initiate this process.[6] Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders,[7] it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. Therefore, we continue to strongly urge the CPSC to hold off on further action until the proper procedures are followed.

Not only is the CPSC disregarding federal law and risking patient privacy, it is also departing from established operating policies. Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction.[8] Based on public reporting the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.[9]

Recently, you told Nextgov/FCW that collecting medical records on vaccines was necessary because the CPSC regulates drug packaging under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. This absurd justification is wrong on its face: PPPA was enacted to require the use of child-resistant packaging, primarily for household products.[10] While the law includes certain medications, such as common over the counter drugs, that could pose a hazard to children if they are not appropriately packaged, patients are not shopping for vaccines and taking them home, where they could be accidentally tampered with by a child. You also did not provide any evidence to back up your claim that there have been reported poisoning incidents involving vaccines that were not in child-resistant packaging.[11] Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be “quite lethal”, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.[12]

Further, we are deeply concerned that these changes under NEISS-R could impact agency rulemaking procedures and outcomes. Major changes to the NEISS could fundamentally reshape how safety rules are prioritized, justified and litigated. NEISS is designed to represent a statistical sample of injury data from across U.S. that the CPSC has used to estimate national injuries and deaths, as well as support rulemakings. It is unclear how this new system will provide comparable nationally representative data and whether differences in methodology and data collection could hamper future rulemakings that require demonstrable risk over time. Consumer safety from hazardous products hinges on strong agency rules that hold industries accountable. It is critical that the agency provide honest and transparent information to the public regarding this matter.

The need for transparency is increasingly important given the use of AI in analyzing patients’ personal information and medical data. Konza Health, the CPSC’s contractor for this project, has claimed it will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities” to automatically filter and transmit the massive amount of data collected from hospitals to the CPSC.”[13] Additionally, a spokesperson from the CPSC shared that after receiving the information from Konza Health, the CPSC would use AI to conduct data analysis and identify trends. Given the role that AI will play in the NEISS-R and the fact that Konza Health could be responsible for storing and securing large swaths of user medical data, it is imperative that the public receive a full account of what technologies and software they will use to comply with this initiative.[14] This is especially important because neither Konza Health nor the CPSC have confirmed if patients will be asked to consent to having their information shared. The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data.[15]

Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R, including strong oversight of Konza Health. The CPSC has claimed that the final architecture of the NEISS-R has not yet been determined since the CPSC does not expect to finalize the NEISS-R until 2027. If that is indeed true, this means that hospitals have been solicited for participation and asked to consent to data sharing requirements before the CPSC can even answer basic questions about the new system. If the CPSC is committed to honesty and transparency, implementation of the NIESS-R must be publicly halted until the CPSC, Congress, and the public have an understanding of the full scope and impact of these updates. To achieve this, we request answers to the following questions by November 19th, 2026:

Will the CPSC require consent from patients prior to the use of their medical data for the NEISS-R system?

How will the CPSC use AI to analyze and sort the data collected from hospitals?

Konza Health has claimed that they are not using AI. Please describe how Konza Health will perform its obligations under its contract and whether it includes the use of AI.

Will any Personally Identifiable Information (PII) obtained through NEISS-R be used to train AI software?

If using a third-party AI product not hosted by the CPSC, will PII be used as an input or otherwise exposed to the model?

What restrictions, if any, does the CPSC plan to implement on transferal of PII to any third party?

Please provide a detailed description of any current or future plans to share NEISS-R data with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

Please specify what type of data analyses Konza Health will conduct that require the use of PII.

Please explain why the analyses cannot be done with data that has been anonymized and/or aggregated before Konza has access.

How will changes to data collection methodologies impact the CPSC’s ability to extrapolate trends or use the data for rulemaking?

How will the CPSC ensure the statistical validity of the system if hospitals select not to respond to the request for information?

As stated above, you recently defended the CPSC’s decision to collect vaccine information because of the CPSC’s oversight of the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. Please explain how the PPPA applies to vaccines administered in a health care setting.

Please provide a detailed list of incidents related to the “poisonings associated with… pharmaceutical packaging that doesn't meet specific child-resistant special packaging requirements” that you alluded to in your statement.

Please provide a detailed explanation of any staffing changes planned to accommodate NEISS-R and the expanded use of AI.

What support is the CPSC providing to hospitals to meet its request for information?

Does the CPSC plan to issue a System of Records Notice or to publish the proposal for public comment as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act? If so, when and if not, please explain why?

Every once in a while, I don’t wear my Senate pin, even if it means I’m going to get stopped on the way in.

I wear this pin.

It’s my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and he spent those 60 years keeping people’s lights on and working to keep their electricity bills affordable.

A little over a month ago, Senator Whitehouse and myself announced, along with our Republican colleagues, our bipartisan permitting bill.

And today, just one week after Americans sent a pretty resounding message about their priorities, we are taking our first vote on that legislation.

And that message that the people sent was pretty clear: they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.

BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm.

This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers.

That one provision is worth $35 billion dollars to American households.

That’s pretty remarkable.

BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion.

And BAAJA will cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and fewer healthcare costs.

This bill’s not perfect.

We’ve never pretended it was.

It is, after all, bipartisan, and that means that neither side got everything they want.

We had to find common ground.

We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.

But bipartisanship doesn’t mean we stop listening, and it doesn’t mean we stop working to make the legislation better.

I have worked hard to incorporate the feedback that we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into our Manager’s Amendment, and I want to walk you through a few of those changes because they’re pretty important.

First, on Tribal consultation, I’ve heard directly from Tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands.

We work to strengthen that dramatically in this Manager’s Amendment.

Tribes will now have an equal seat with states in transmission planning, and federal agencies will be required, and let me say that again: required “shall” consult, not “may” consult, “shall” consult early with Tribes on projects that will affect important cultural sites, including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harms, and basically that means that mandatory Tribal consultation is now built into every single step of the Section 106 process by law.

We’ve also extended the window for objections to agency reports.

We’ve strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, and we’ve given states a way to ask FERC to investigate local utility projects that gouge consumers.

That, in my view, is particularly important as private equity and other outside investors seek to take a larger role in electric utilities.

States need the tools to protect their ratepayers.

Third, we’ve made sure that workers’ rights are protected.

The Manager’s Amendment preserves collective bargaining agreements for union employees of the power of bargaining administrations, so that those workers can continue to bargain collectively and stand up for workers’ rights.

And finally, we’ve added a new Department of Energy Data Center Community Assistance Program because when a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, costs, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision.

This program will give state, local, and Tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions.

These are meaningful improvements.

They reflect the feedback that we’ve heard and they make an important piece of legislation, in my view, even stronger.

And importantly, they don’t change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure that data centers pay their fair share.

That’s what we set out to accomplish when we started this project, and that’s what we’re still working to deliver.

So I would urge all my colleagues: Let’s get this done.

Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again.

The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives.

We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs.

We can do that today.

So let’s pass permitting reform.

Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-04) raised concerns about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) abrupt decision to halt funding for the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance (WIPA) program’s National Training and Data Center (NTDC) at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), threatening critical services that help Americans with disabilities navigate Social Security benefits while seeking employment.

The NTDC provides training, certification, and technical assistance to more than 900 benefits counselors serving individuals with disabilities across the country. On October 2, 2026, SSA abruptly declined to fund VCU’s contract for another year and ordered the university to immediately halt work, disrupting essential training and support services for 74 WIPA projects nationwide.

In a letter to SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano, the lawmakers demanded an explanation for the decision and pressed the agency to clarify how it intends to restore these critical services and fulfill its statutory obligations.

The lawmakers wrote, “We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.”

The WIPA program helps individuals who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) due to severe, long-term medical conditions understand how employment may affect their benefits. Benefits counselors provide free, individualized guidance to help Americans with disabilities pursue employment opportunities without inadvertently jeopardizing the benefits they rely on.

The lawmakers continued, “CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.”

Despite Congress appropriating $23 million for the WIPA program in Fiscal Year 2026, SSA’s decision has left benefits counselors nationwide without access to necessary training resources, certification services, performance data, and institutional knowledge. These resources are critical to training new counselors and ensuring that both new and existing counselors provide accurate, reliable guidance to Americans with disabilities. The sudden loss of these services raises serious concerns about SSA’s ability to meet its statutory obligations and ensure that beneficiaries continue receiving the support they need.

The lawmakers pressed SSA to explain the rationale and timing of its decision, identify what training and certification resources remain available to benefits counselors, address disruptions to required performance reporting, and clarify whether the agency intends to restore these services through VCU, bring them in-house, or award a new contract.

Dear Commissioner Bisignano,

We write to inquire about the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) decision to defund the Work Incentives Planning and Assistance program’s (WIPA) National Training and Data Center (NTDC). We are aware that on Friday, October 2, 2026, the SSA exercised its option not to extend its contract with Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) to administer the NTDC and ordered VCU to immediately halt all work providing Community Work Incentives Coordinators (CWICs) nationwide with training, certification, technical assistance, and other resource support.

Disabled beneficiaries who qualify for SSDI or SSI benefits are among the most vulnerable populations who suffer from severe, long-term medical conditions. To maintain compliance, beneficiaries must navigate a series of strict and complex requirements set out by the Social Security Act, including on earned income. For beneficiaries who need to earn extra income to support themselves or their families, incorrectly interpreting the rules can lead to a termination of benefits.

The Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 directed the Commissioner of Social Security to establish a program to provide information about work and benefits to people who receive Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because of a disability. Using that authority, SSA established 74 WIPA projects in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. WIPA projects and community organizations employ over 900 benefits counselors who provide free in-depth counseling to disabled beneficiaries on the effect of work on their SSDI or SSI benefits.

CWICs at WIPA projects help bridge the information gap for beneficiaries by looking at their individual circumstances and advising them on how to maintain their benefits while working. To ensure the efficacy of the WIPA programs, the law also required SSA to establish a corps of work incentives specialists and provide training and technical assistance for those specialists. CWICs provide information and resources to help beneficiaries make informed decisions on returning to work.

In Fiscal Year 2026 Congress appropriated $23 million to operate the WIPA program, 0.1 percent of SSA’s annual administrative budget. However, despite clear Congressional intent in support of the WIPA program, SSA has decided to unilaterally disband a vital component of the program. Without the NTDC, WIPA projects nationwide have lost access to valuable training resources and performance data to train new CWICs and ensure both new and existing Coordinators provide accurate and relevant information to beneficiaries. WIPA projects are also losing access to an invaluable source of institutional knowledge.

After this abrupt decision, it is unclear how SSA intends to comply with the statutory requirements of the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999 and Congressional intent set out in the Fiscal Year 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act.

We request answers to the following questions by November 16, 2026:

Why was the decision made to defund NTDC? Please provide a full account of the facts that informed the decision to defund NTDC.

When was the final decision made to defund NTDC? When were NTDC staff and VCU staff informed of the decision?

What training resources, if any, do WIPA projects have access to following the closure of the NTDC?

WIPA projects are required to submit its quarterly performance data at the end of this month. The performance data WIPA projects submit to maintain grantee status was collected and tracked through the WIPA STAR system. Given the sudden cancellation of the WIPA STAR system, will the reporting deadline be extended?

To obtain/maintain certification, CWICs were required to receive training through VCU. How will CWICs now receive certification training? Will SSA waive certification requirements if CWICs are unable to access the training?

Will SSA bring the training and technical assistance previously performed by VCU in-house? If not, does SSA plan on issuing a recompete of the contract?

Letter Text (PDF)

Washington (November 9, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, today wrote to Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet Inc. and Google, demanding the company reverse its policy to block access to Google Search on K-12 student accounts at schools that want to disable artificial intelligence (AI) services, including Gemini, Google’s AI chatbot. AI chatbots are often designed to encourage compulsive use and emotional attachment exposing children to risks of manipulation and, in some more serious cases, have resulted in chatbots encouraging children to die by suicide. Google should not use its dominant position in the education technology market to force schools to adopt potentially dangerous AI technologies or risk losing a critical research tool like Google Search.

In the letter, Senator Markey wrote, “Just this month, a girl and her family sued Google after Gemini allegedly ‘helped coach her through a plan to commit suicide.’ The girl accessed Gemini through Google Search on a school-issued Chromebook, even though the school had blocked access to Gemini’s standalone app and website. At a time when schools, parents, and policymakers are working hard to implement safeguards on AI chatbots for our children, Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage. Schools deserve the right to block student access to AI chatbots without also forfeiting access to an important educational tool.”

Senator Markey continued, “Google’s dominant position in education technology makes this ultimatum particularly concerning. Although Google has a right to create and offer new educational tools, it should not use its dominant market position to force schools to adopt them.”

Senator Markey requested the following information by November 30, 2026:

Will Google commit to allowing schools to disable generative AI features and chatbots on K-12 student accounts, including AI Overviews, Gemini, and Guided Learning, while retaining access to Google Search?

Is it technically feasible for Google to provide K-12 student accounts with Google Search results that exclude AI Overviews, Guided Learning, and other generative AI features or chatbots?

Please provide any research, testing, or risk assessments that Google has conducted on the safety, mental health, and learning effects of AI Overviews, Gemini, and Guided Learning on K-12 students, including for children under age 13.

How many K-12 schools and districts that use Google’s products currently restrict or prohibit students’ access to generative AI features or AI chatbots outside Google Search?

Washington (November 9, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, released the following statement on the Senate’s vote to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026.

“We need to stop the Trump administration’s weaponization of our government against clean, affordable, and ready-to-go energy sources, and we need to build an energy grid that works for Americans now and into the future—that means cutting emissions and cutting costs. But as currently drafted, this bill attempts to address these goals by asking communities to trade the benefits of interstate transmission and the ability to make data centers pay more for grid power for the sacrifices of weakened clean water protections, intrusion on sovereign Tribal rights, and limits on the ability to be heard and considered during federal approval of projects ranging from hyperscale data centers to petrochemical plants. Legal experts have also raised serious concerns about the potential unintended effects of provisions that are meant to prevent Trump’s misuse of the permitting process but could impair environmental protections into the future at taxpayers’ expense. And without a committee process and sufficient time to work through and resolve these tradeoffs and questions, we do not have the answers we need.

“Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership. I believe we owe it to them to fight to win a better deal that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.

“Because of these issues on timing, transparency, and threats to our clean air, water, and Tribes, I will vote against the motion to invoke cloture on this legislation. I will continue to discuss all these issues with my colleagues, both in the coming days and into the next Congress, and hope to work toward a better deal in the future.”

Washington, DC – Today, Oregon’s Senator Jeff Merkley released the following statement on proposed legislation in the Senate to reform permitting:

“Transmission is much needed to move renewable energy from solar and wind farms to the places where there is a high demand for electricity.

“Data centers should pay their fair share for the resources they use.

“And having cleaner, cheaper renewable energy is important for reducing energy costs here at home, for our country’s competitive status in the world, and for our ability to tackle climate chaos.

“I strongly support the portions of this bill that seek these outcomes and praise the work of my colleagues – Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich – who have strived to accomplish these objectives.

“But at the demand of the fossil fuel titans, this bill also accelerates the extraction and burning of fossil fuels.

“Very simply: getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that.

“This bill could make it easier to build more data centers powered by ‘behind the meter’ natural gas plants.

“It makes it much easier to build natural gas pipelines that will transport incredible quantities of natural gas overseas as LNG.

“More pipelines and export terminals equal more American fracked gas burned at home and abroad.

“And while the models exclude American gas burned abroad from the climate impact of this bill, the Earth is affected the same no matter where the gas is burned.

“This bill has a number of other features that merit careful analysis. Yet, the bill has never had a public hearing. Not in the House. Not in the Senate.

“Robust consideration of the bill should be a priority in the new Congress.

“Here are some of the other issues that merit careful examination.

“The bill restricts states’ ability to raise and address clean water concerns on gas pipelines as well as transmission lines.

“It shortens timelines that make it hard-to-impossible for grassroots and community groups to raise concerns about projects.

“It eliminates tools that states and localities use to fight the development of new data centers and detention centers.

“And it impacts the sovereignty and rights of Tribes.

“Permitting reform for electrical transmission lines is essential.

“But the current bill raises too many serious issues that require more deliberation.

“I will vote against the bill before us today, but I look forward to working with my colleagues to get permitting reform right.”

“The need for a permitting reform package has only grown in the past decade, as bureaucracy has stymied the development of vital projects from clean energy to housing that could lower costs. And I appreciate the work done by Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich to negotiate a bipartisan agreement, as a lasting solution can only be reached by reaching across the aisle. In particular, the transmission and grid reform provisions are very positive. And the changes that they secured in the manager’s amendment make this a better bill. Nevertheless, the bill needs further improvement before I can support it.

“My top priorities in such an agreement are to bring down energy bills through new clean energy development, to lower emission rates, to support tribal sovereignty, and to stop the administration from attacking American clean energy projects. This includes restoring the billions of dollars in terminated energy projects in California, as well as the offshore wind projects the administration baselessly and illegally canceled. The president’s comments today, that notwithstanding any compromise in this bill, he intends to continue blocking wind projects, demonstrate a singular but telling lack of good faith. I have said from the start that we need to have confidence that any permitting reform legislation is not going to be weaponized by this or any future administration to single out states and provide giveaways to the oil and gas industries. In its current form, this bill does not satisfy those priorities and raises other serious concerns.

“This legislation would jeopardize tribal sovereignty through major changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, impact the State of California’s authorities under the Clean Water Act, and constrict federal agencies’ ability to protect vulnerable wildlife under the Endangered Species Act. While I support the provisions in this bill that require data center companies to cover the costs of grid infrastructure and protect American taxpayers from footing the bill — which mirror my legislation — the legislation overall contains too many giveaways to oil and gas with insufficient constraints on an energy policy that has prioritized corporate profit over the pocketbooks of hard-working Americans and public health. Washington, D.C. (11/10/2026): Today, Rep. Burchett introduced the Community Control of Data Centers Act. The recent boom in AI has made data centers a central component of infrastructure that may have major economic implications. Despite potential benefits, it is important that the decision to build them should be made by the Americans who live in those towns, not Washington bureaucrats and Big Tech CEOs.
