Washington, D.C. — In case you missed it, Congressman Rich McCormick (GA-07) recently wrote an op-ed in The Hill highlighting his newly introduced Common-Sense Cloud Security Act and the urgent need to modernize America's cybersecurity standards as threats to our critical infrastructure continue to evolve.

The legislation directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to update cloud security guidance, strengthen cyber risk assessments, and establish a voluntary certification program to help organizations better prevent, detect, and contain cyberattacks. In the op-ed, McCormick emphasized that protecting America's digital infrastructure requires more than keeping hackers out. It means limiting the damage they can cause once inside, ensuring a single breach cannot compromise an entire network.

“The key challenge is not simply keeping attackers out. It’s limiting what they can do when they get in,” McCormick wrote.

McCormick underscored the importance of practical, risk-based security standards that protect the hospitals, businesses, financial institutions, and government agencies Americans rely on every day without slowing American innovation.

You can read the full op-ed in The Hill or below.

Image

America has embraced cloud computing at a remarkable pace with nearly every aspect of life now running through the cloud. Businesses, hospitals, banks, and government agencies rely on cloud services to store data, run operations, and deliver critical services. As our reliance grows, so does our exposure to cyber threats. The very innovation that has transformed our economy has also created new vulnerabilities that demand our attention.

That’s why I introduced the Common-Sense Cloud Security Act. This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for securing cloud environments and assessing cyber risk in ways that reflect how modern systems actually operate.

The key challenge is not simply keeping attackers out. It’s limiting what they can do when they get in.

Think of a cloud network like a building. Strong locks, passwords, and identity checks keep intruders out. But security also depends on what happens inside. An intruder should not be able to walk into every room, access every file, or reach every critical system. The same principle applies in the cloud.

For far too long, cybersecurity has focused on preventing a breach without giving enough attention to containing one. In today’s increasingly interconnected environments, one compromised account or application should not put an entire network at risk.

Resilience matters just as much as prevention.

As a Marine Corps veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, I know firsthand that military and national security depend on the strength of the systems behind them. My work on the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee and the House AI Task Force have reinforced a critical lesson: American innovation and digital security must advance together. As technology evolves, so must our ability to protect it.

Security experts often use the term “blast radius” to describe how far an attack can spread and how much damage it can cause. A single compromised account, application or service should not become a gateway to an entire organization. Effective cybersecurity is not just about detecting threats. It is about containing them. Measuring and reducing that risk provides a more meaningful assessment of security than simply determining whether suspicious activity can be detected.

The rise of super intelligence (formerly, “artificial intelligence”) makes this challenge even more urgent. Modern SI systems increasingly interact with multiple applications, databases and services across an organization. While these capabilities can create tremendous productivity and efficiency gains, they can also expand the potential consequences of a compromise. The more authority a system has, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on what it can access.

This is not about slowing innovation with another unnecessary layer of bureaucracy. It is about developing practical, risk-based security standards that reflect how modern cloud systems actually work and giving organizations meaningful ways to demonstrate that they are in compliance.

If effective cybersecurity means limiting the damage caused by a breach, then our standards must reflect that reality. That is why my Common-Sense Cloud Security Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop updated guidance for modern cloud environments, including identity management, oversight of third-party connections, detection of suspicious activity, and ways to assess the potential impact of a compromise. The bill would also establish a voluntary certification program and help ensure federal cloud security requirements keep pace with evolving technology and threats.

No law or standard can eliminate every cyber threat. What we can do is make attacks harder, limit their impact, and improve our ability to recover when they occur.

I will continue working with cybersecurity experts and industry leaders to strengthen the security of the cloud infrastructure Americans rely on every day. In today's interconnected world, security is not measured by whether a breach occurs. It is measured by how well we contain it. WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the urgency of passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. Following Chairman Capito’s remarks, the Senate advanced BAAJA by a vote of 73-25.

Below are the floor remarks of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as prepared for delivery.

“Madam President, for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.

“Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions. Communities nationwide have waited in regulatory limbo for roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities, and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies. All this has led to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities, and higher prices across America.

“Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.

“These are projects that could provide good-paying jobs, improve mobility, increase access to clean drinking water, deploy broadband in rural areas, and so much more. The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can’t be made. This is not a sustainable way for the United States to compete with the rest of the world, and it is certainly not a sustainable way to address the energy and affordability issues we are facing today.

“It’s no secret that America’s energy demand is growing rapidly to meet the needs of a modern economy. To meet these needs, we must modernize our grid, increase our energy production, and build the infrastructure that will keep America competitive and secure for decades to come.

“It is time for Congress to act. It is, actually, well past time.

“As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I worked with my Ranking Member, Senator Whitehouse, as well as Chairman Lee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Ranking Member Heinrich, to introduce a comprehensive permitting reform solution: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA. This bill will unlock economic opportunity, infrastructure development, and energy production across the United States.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts. The first part of the bill is in the EPW Committee’s jurisdiction, and it consists of reforms to the laws that set the framework for our environmental review and permitting processes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The EPWsection also provides certainty that permitted projects will retain their permits if they remain in compliance with the law.

“The second part of the bill captures reforms to statutes in the ENR Committee’s jurisdiction, including the National Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. This section also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of American consumers facing increased costs through rising utility bills.

“Together, the package that our committees put together fulfills key policy priorities from members of both sides of the aisle and a diverse set of stakeholders. I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.

“First, this bill is bipartisan. Senators Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich, and I have worked together throughout this Congress to craft a solution that both Republicans and Democrats can support. That is the only way we can achieve durable and implementable reforms to our environmental review and permitting processes. There is something in this bill for everyone, because it is fair to everyone, and we owe it to the American people to come together as a body and pass this legislation in the weeks ahead.

“Second, this bill will help all types of projects. We cannot adjust the processes for some types of projects, but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

“Third, the package addresses critical stages of the permitting process. This will create predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. It will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy. Finally, our legislation will prevent unnecessary delays and endless litigation that blocks growth.

“In West Virginia, investments have collapsed under the weight of legal challenges, denying potential benefits to areas that need support the most. When a project sits in the environmental review and permitting processes for years, jobs are not created, critical infrastructure is not built, energy is not brought onto the grid, and ultimately, American families and businesses face higher costs and fewer opportunities.

“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear. According to their analysis, the reforms made under BAAJA would result in $82 billion to $164 billion in additional economic output every year. Families would feel these economic benefits directly, as CEA estimates that for the average American household, real wages will increase, electricity bills will fall, and everyday expenses will be reduced. We cannot continue to let the costs of permitting delays fall onto American families.

“I am no stranger to the challenge of addressing permitting reform in Congress. Throughout my career, I have introduced multiple bills to improve this process. While Congress has passed some very limited reforms through various legislative packages, we have not passed significant reforms to NEPA in several decades.

Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. These are not partisan ideals. They are American principles.

“The Trump administration has also rallied behind this deal, supporting our efforts in the Senate to pass durable reforms so we can unleash our nation’s full potential. Additionally, we have made it a priority to have a robust manager’s amendment to this legislation that makes targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support.

“I am thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen BAAJA, and the contributions from members of the House of Representatives as well. This legislation reflects a vast amount of perspectives and priorities, and I’m proud of the product we are voting on today.

“We have received letters of support from over one thousand stakeholder organizations, representing a broad swath of groups across our country, including oil and gas producers and solar energy groups, labor unions, and business associations. They all recognize the urgent need for permitting reform, and the benefits that BAAJA would have on affordability, energy reliability, and economic growth across our country.

“In a statement from the American Petroleum Institute, President and CEO Mike Sommers said, 'Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job.'

“In another statement from the Solar Energy Industries Association, CEO Tim Pawlenty said, 'This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses.'

“Xan Fishman, Executive Vice President of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said, '[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes.'

“From my home state, the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia’s President, Rebecca McPhail, said the following, 'GO-WV supports the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act]’s stated goals of modernizing federal environmental review, providing certainty for holders of federal permits and authorizations, and supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.'

“From the business community, Rodney Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of Government Affairs at the U.S. Chamber, said, 'The Senate's progress toward a comprehensive, bipartisan permitting reform deal brings us one step closer to streamlining the outdated process that is holding up critical projects of all kinds, from energy and water infrastructure to roads, broadband, and manufacturing.’

“Demonstrating the breadth of support this bill has received, the Laborers’ International Union of North America General President, Brent Booker, gave the following statement of support, 'For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills…We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform.'

“And finally, representing a broad coalition of labor groups, in a letter from Sean McGarvey, President of North America’s Building Trades Unions, he said, 'This legislation represents a significant step toward a more efficient permitting system that supports job creation, strengthens America’s energy and infrastructure capabilities, and helps reduce costs for working families.'

“I could not agree more. This is an unprecedented opportunity, and a legislative breakthrough we can accomplish in this unique moment. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.

“The reality is this: over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production and manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand, and that means making sure our infrastructure projects can be built quickly, efficiently, and responsibly.

“The House has already passed several key pieces of legislation on this matter, including the SPEED Act and the PERMIT Act. Now, it’s our turn in the Senate to act on the opportunity in front of us. I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“American growth, competitiveness, and security are at stake. With that, I yield the floor.”

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-LA) today recommended Brad Kelley to the Senate Judiciary Committee for consideration as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana. Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member,

It is my privilege to recommend Brad Kelley to the Committee to be a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana.

Brad’s record reflects academic excellence, distinguished military service, significant public service, and sophisticated legal practice. Brad is a proud double-graduate of LSU, where he graduated, summa cum laude, with degrees in Political Science, History, and International Studies. In recognition of his academic achievement, he was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa.

Brad later attended LSU’s Paul M. Hebert Law Center, where he was an editor of both the Louisiana Law Review and the Journal of Civil Law Studies. Brad received his law degree, magna cum laude, and was inducted into the Order of the Coif.

Following law school, Brad clerked for the Honorable Donald E. Walter of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, where he gained a rare view into the inner workings of a federal court.

If confirmed, Brad will take an Oath to uphold the Constitution. He knows something about that firsthand. Between college and law school, he served our country honorably as a captain in the United States Army. Brad served as an infantry platoon leader and as a lead intelligence officer for a unit of nearly one thousand soldiers. During the Iraq War, he also advised senior command leadership on combat missions.

Brad’s commitment to those who serve did not end when he left the Army. As an attorney, he provides regular legal assistance and counsel to Gold Star Families––those special Americans who have suffered the grievous loss of immediate family killed in the line of duty. In addition to helping the families of those who have fallen, Brad has aided those who live on with the wounds of their service. In recognition of his extensive pro bono work on behalf of our veterans, Brad received a commendation.

Brad also brings substantial experience in public service. After a stint in private practice, Brad returned to government service, where he served as a senior official during both Republican and Democrat administrations, including as a Senior Policy Advisor at the U.S. Department of Labor and as Chief Counsel to a Commissioner of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). Those positions gave him firsthand experience with federal law, administrative agencies, and the practical consequences of government decision-making.

Brad then returned to private practice, where he became an equity partner at one of the world’s largest labor and employment law firms. He now co-chairs the firm’s artificial intelligence and technology practice group and has served as lead counsel in complex litigation across the country.

That breadth of experience matters. Our federal district courts benefit from exposure to how difficult legal issues have been settled in other circuits, in addition to their own. Brad’s cross-jurisdictional experience makes him apt for this task. He is admitted to the practice of law in Louisiana, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. He is also admitted to the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Third, Fourth, Fifth, and D.C. Circuits.

And Brad is no stranger to the court on which he has been nominated to serve. He has litigated several matters in the Eastern District of Louisiana, including matters as recently as this year.

Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member, I am confident that Brad Kelley has the credentials, experience, rigor, and patriotism that mark exceptional nominees to the federal bench. I support his nomination without question.

With that, I yield.

“And we are—every single one of us—ready to meet this moment.”

Dear Majority Leader Thune, Minority Leader Schumer, Speaker Johnson, Minority Leader Jeffries, Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, Chairman Rogers, and Ranking Member Smith:

As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to exclude three provisions from the final bill that would further entrench concerning aspects of the U.S.-Israel defense and intelligence relationship at a time when the Israeli government’s actions are increasingly undermining U.S. interests and values. These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.

Both Section 1217 from the Senate Armed Services Committee-reported bill and Section 219 of the House-passed bill mandate the creation of a “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” to expand and accelerate the U.S.-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare such as biotechnology, quantum, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and others.

The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests. Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest.

If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.

Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values.

Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, “I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.” The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests.

In addition to the provisions discussed above in the Senate and House NDAAs, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI) FY27 Intelligence Authorization Act, which is typically incorporated in the final NDAA, includes a provision (Sec. 618) that mandates the executive branch “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel,” and also states that intelligence sharing with Israel “shall not be suspended, reduced, or otherwise materially limited.” The provision would tie the President’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect U.S. national security. That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level.

For all these reasons, we should not legally mandate an expansion in defense co-production or a requirement to increase intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. We therefore urge you to exclude Section 1217, Section 219, and Section 618 from the NDAA final conference report.
